title: Ease in crochet garments
subtitle: Understanding positive and negative ease, and how crochet fabric changes after blocking
excerpt: Ease is the difference between your body measurement and the finished garment size. Most crochet garments are designed with positive ease, meaning the garment is wider than the body and hangs with a relaxed fit. Choosing the wrong size happens when you match your body measurement to the pattern's finished size rather than to your body measurement on the size chart.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: When the finished garment measures more than the body at the same point. The garment hangs loosely from the body rather than fitting against it. Most crochet garments use positive ease.
When the finished garment measures less than the body at the same point. The garment must stretch to fit, giving a snug result. Used in hats, tube tops, and stretchy-stitch garments.
The measurement around the fullest part of the chest, taken parallel to the floor. The key body measurement for sizing upper-body crochet garments.

content.text: Positive ease
is the extra room built into most crochet garments. A jumper sized for a 90 cm
bust circumference
might have a finished chest measurement of 100 cm. The 10 cm difference is the ease. It gives the garment drape, room to move, and the relaxed look that most crochet fabric is suited to.

The mistake most often made when choosing a crochet garment size is comparing body measurements directly to the finished garment size on the schematic. This gives the wrong size. Compare body measurements to the body measurement column in the size table instead. Let the pattern design the ease.
What you need

items.name: Flexible measuring tape
items.note: For taking your own measurements. Ask someone to help with back-waist measurements, which are hard to take accurately alone.

content.text: Types of ease
Most crochet garments use positive ease. The amount varies by design intention:
Close fit: 2.5 to 5 cm of ease. The garment follows the body shape.
Standard fit: 7.5 to 12.5 cm of ease. The usual range for jumpers and cardigans.
Relaxed fit: 12.5 to 20 cm of ease. Oversized garments, loose tops, and most crochet blanket cardigans.
Negative ease

is less common in crochet than in knitting because crochet fabric is generally less elastic. It appears in hats (where the brim must grip the head), tube tops in stretchy stitch patterns, and garments worked in ribbing or other textured stitches that recover their shape after stretching.
How blocking changes the fit

Crochet fabric can grow after wet blocking, sometimes substantially. A lace cardigan worked in cotton can gain 3 to 5 cm in width after its first wash. A dense double crochet (UK) garment in wool will change very little. The pattern's finished measurements should be post-blocking dimensions.

Before starting a garment, wet-block the gauge swatch and measure it in its blocked state. If your gauge swatch matches the pattern's stated gauge after blocking, the finished garment will match the schematic. If it does not match, the garment will not come out in the stated size regardless of which size you choose.
Taking your own measurements
Bust or chest: measure around the fullest part of the chest, keeping the tape parallel to the floor and relaxed, not pulled tight.
Waist: measure around the narrowest part of the torso, above the hip bones.
Hip: measure around the fullest part of the hips, usually 20 to 23 cm below the waist.
Back length: measure from the bony point at the back of the neck to the natural waist.
Sleeve length: measure from the shoulder point (where the seam would sit) to the wrist bone, with the arm slightly bent.
Common problems

items.symptom: The finished garment is much too large even though the right size was chosen
items.cause: Gauge was not checked, or the yarn grew more than expected after blocking.
items.fix: Block the swatch before starting the next garment and verify gauge in the blocked state. If the pattern does not say whether the gauge is pre- or post-blocking, assume post-blocking.

items.symptom: The garment fits at the chest but is very long in the body
items.cause: Row gauge is different from the pattern, or the body length was not checked against the schematic mid-project.
items.fix: Measure the body piece against the schematic at the armhole point before starting armhole shaping. Stop early or work extra rows as needed.

items.symptom: The garment fits everywhere except it feels tight across the upper back
items.cause: Back width and bust width are not the same for all bodies. A standard-size chart may fit the bust measurement but not the shoulder width.
items.fix: When choosing a size by chest measurement, also check the shoulder width on the schematic. If the pattern offers multiple measurements, choose the size where the shoulder width works best.

content.text: What to try next

Find a pattern with a detailed schematic before starting. Take your measurements. Locate your size on the size chart. Read the ease statement and decide whether to size up or down. This step-by-step practice makes size selection fast and reliable.
